incidente.resumo: While manually re-synchronising a lagging PostgreSQL secondary, the database directory was wiped on the primary instead of the secondary, removing around 300 GB of data; GitLab.com was down for about 18 hours and database changes made after 17:20 UTC were lost because pg_dump backups had been failing silently and disk snapshots were not enabled for the database servers. Service was restored by copying the data directory from a 6-hour-old LVM snapshot in staging to production and then restoring webhooks from a separate database.

descricao.texto: The wipe was noticed by the engineer running it, who terminated the process a second or two later, by which point around 300 GB of data had already been removed.
trechos: The engineer terminated the process a second or two after noticing their mistake, but at this point around 300 GB of data had already been removed.

gatilho.texto: Trying to restore the replication process, the PostgreSQL database directory was wiped on the primary instead of the secondary, in the belief that it was the secondary; around 300 GB of data was removed before the process was terminated.
trechos: Trying to restore the replication process, an engineer proceeds to wipe the PostgreSQL database directory, errantly thinking they were doing so on the secondary.
Unfortunately this process was executed on the primary instead.
The engineer terminated the process a second or two after noticing their mistake, but at this point around 300 GB of data had already been removed.

descricao.texto: Replication to the secondary failed because WAL segments it needed had already been removed from the primary, and without WAL archiving the secondary had to be re-synchronised manually by removing its data directory and running pg_basebackup; this restoration required manual work because it was not automated nor documented properly.
trechos: The replication failed as WAL segments needed by the secondary were already removed from the primary.
As GitLab.com was not using WAL archiving, the secondary had to be re-synchronised manually.

Database replication stopped,
requiring the secondary to be reset/rebuilt.

Restoring this required manual work as
this was not automated, nor was it documented properly.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: From around 19:00 UTC database load increased, which the authors suspect was due to spam, together with a background job removing an employee account that had been flagged for abuse and accidentally scheduled for removal; due to the increased load the secondary's replication started to lag around 23:00 UTC.
trechos:
**± 19:00 UTC:** GitLab.com starts experiencing an increase in database load due
to what we suspect was spam.
We would later find out that part of the load was caused by a background job trying to remove a GitLab employee and their associated data.
This was the result of their account being flagged for abuse and accidentally scheduled for removal.

**± 23:00 UTC:** Due to the increased load, our PostgreSQL secondary's
replication process started to lag behind.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: pg_basebackup appeared to hang silently; this is normal behaviour while it waits for the primary to send replication data, but it was not clearly documented in the engineering runbooks nor in the official pg_basebackup documentation.
trechos:
Unfortunately `pg_basebackup` would hang, producing no
meaningful output, despite the `--verbose` option being set.

this is normal behaviour: `pg_basebackup` will wait for the primary to start
sending over replication data and it will sit and wait silently until that time.

Unfortunately this was not clearly documented in our engineering
runbooks nor in the official
`pg_basebackup` document.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The daily pg_dump backups were not working: the procedure ran on an application server with no PostgreSQL data directory, so the Omnibus package defaulted to pg_dump 9.2 while the database ran PostgreSQL 9.6, and pg_dump terminated with an error; the S3 bucket was empty.
trechos: The S3 bucket was empty, and there was no recent backup to be found anywhere.

Upon closer inspection we found out that the backup procedure was using
`pg_dump` 9.2, while our database is running PostgreSQL 9.6 (for Postgres, 9.x
releases are considered major).

The `pg_dump` procedure was executed on a regular application server, not the
database server.

As a result there is no PostgreSQL data directory present on
these servers, thus Omnibus defaults to PostgreSQL 9.2.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Cronjob failure notifications were sent by email, but DMARC was not enabled for the cronjob emails, so they were rejected by the receiver and the backup failures went unnoticed; the backup procedure was also not tested regularly because it had no owner.
trechos: While notifications are enabled for any cronjobs that error, these notifications are sent by email.
Unfortunately DMARC was not enabled for the cronjob emails, resulting in them being rejected by the receiver.
This means we were never aware of the backups failing, until it was too late.

**Why was the backup procedure not tested on a regular basis?** - Because
there was no ownership, as a result nobody was responsible for testing this
procedure.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Azure disk snapshots were enabled for the NFS servers but not for any database servers, because the other backup procedures were assumed to be sufficient.
trechos: While enabled for the NFS servers, these snapshots were not enabled for any of the database servers as we assumed that our other backup procedures were sufficient enough.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: Restoration had to use the staging database on Azure classic without Premium Storage; its network disks were throttled to around 60Mbps and copying the data from staging to production took around 18 hours.
trechos: For our staging environment we were using Azure classic, without Premium Storage.
As a result the disks are very slow, resulting in them being the main bottleneck in the restoration process.
Copying the data from the staging to the production host took around 18 hours.
These disks are network disks and are throttled to a really low number (around 60Mbps), there is no way to move from cheap storage to premium, so this was the performance we would get out of it.

passos.texto: The LVM snapshot created manually about 6 hours before the outage was chosen for recovery, and the PostgreSQL data directory was copied from the staging host to the production host, which took around 18 hours; the database was then restored to its state at January 31st, 17:20 UTC.
trechos: To recover GitLab.com we decided to use the LVM snapshot created 6 hours before the outage, as it was our only option to reduce data loss as much as possible (the alternative was to lose almost 24 hours of data).
Since copying over and restoring the data directory would be easier we decided to go with this solution.
Copying the data from the staging to the production host took around 18 hours.
Once copied we were able to restore the database (including webhooks) to the state it was at January 31st, 17:20 UTC.

passos.texto: On February 1st at 17:00 UTC the GitLab.com database was restored without webhooks; webhooks were restored by creating a separate staging database from the LVM snapshot without triggering webhook removal, generating a SQL dump of the table and importing it into the restored database, with final restoration finished around 18:00 UTC.
trechos: On February 1st at 17:00 UTC we managed to restore the GitLab.com database without webhooks.
Restoring webhooks was done by creating a separate staging database using the LVM snapshot, but without triggering the removal of webhooks.
This allowed us to generate a SQL dump of the table and import this into the restored GitLab.com database.
Around 18:00 UTC we finished the final restoration procedures such as restoring the webhooks and confirming everything was operating as expected.

passos.texto: Projects created after 17:20 were restored in their most basic form from their Git repositories still stored in the NFS cluster, without associated data such as issues and merge requests.
trechos: We ran a procedure to restore these projects based on their Git repositories that were still stored in our NFS cluster.
This procedure however was only able to restore projects in their most basic form, without associated data such as issues and merge requests.

acoes.texto: Already done: LVM snapshots are now taken every hour instead of once per 24 hours.
trechos:

**Problem 1:** GitLab.com was down for about 18 hours.

perguntas_em_aberto: The exact amount of data lost is hard to estimate; the estimate is at least 5000 projects, 5000 comments and roughly 700 users.

observacoes: The text gives two windows for the lost data: 17:20 to 00:00 UTC in the introduction and 17:20 to 23:30 UTC in the data loss section. The 5 Whys also states that restoring GitLab.com took over 18 hours. Also noted in the text: max_connections had been set to 8000 almost a year earlier and had to be reduced to 2000 for PostgreSQL to restart during the incident.
